content: An alcohol rub, commonly referred to as hand sanitizer or healthcare personnel hand wash, is utilized as a supplementary or alternative method to traditional handwashing with soap and water. The active components in alcohol rubs typically include isopropanol, ethanol, or, in some European formulations, propanol. These products are available in various forms, such as gels, foams, and liquid solutions. Alcohol-based hand sanitizers are generally more effective at eliminating microorganisms compared to soap and are less likely to cause skin dryness. When hands are not visibly soiled, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recognizes alcohol-based hand sanitizers as an acceptable substitute for soap and water in maintaining hand hygiene. For these products to effectively kill microbes, the alcohol concentration must exceed 60%. However, research conducted at East Tennessee State University has revealed that some products with alcohol concentrations as low as 40% are available in the United States, which are less effective. The optimal alcohol concentration for germicidal activity ranges between 70% and 95%. Alcohol gels containing 62% alcohol by volume (v/v) are less effective at killing germs compared to alcohol rubs with at least 70% alcohol by weight (wt/wt). Formulations that combine alcohol with additional antimicrobial agents, such as benzalkonium chloride, demonstrate significantly enhanced efficacy compared to alcohol alone. Most alcohol rubs also include moisturizers to prevent excessive skin dryness. Alcohol rubs are capable of killing a wide range of bacteria, including antibiotic-resistant strains and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. They are also effective against many viruses, such as influenza and the common cold virus, as well as fungi. However, not all pathogens are equally susceptible to alcohol-based sanitizers. For instance, spore-forming gram-positive bacteria, such as Clostridium difficile, exhibit relative resistance and can remain viable. During the anthrax attacks on the United States Postal Service, authorities explicitly warned that alcohol-based hand rubs would not be effective against anthrax spores. Additionally, in environments with high levels of lipids or protein waste, such as food processing facilities, alcohol rubs alone may not provide adequate hand hygiene. Alcohol-based hand sanitizers are flammable due to their alcohol content and can produce a faint blue flame when ignited. Some formulations with higher water or moisturizer content may not exhibit this effect. Although rare, there have been documented cases where alcohol-based hand sanitizers have been implicated in fires, including incidents where static electricity ignited the product. To mitigate fire risks, users are advised to rub their hands until the sanitizer has completely dried, indicating that the alcohol has evaporated. Furthermore, ingestion of alcohol-based hand sanitizers can result in alcohol poisoning, particularly in young children. In the United States, over 12,000 cases of child-related alcohol poisoning have been directly linked to hand sanitizer products.
